newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli shares close higher on blue chip rise.
newsitem.headline: Israeli shares close higher on blue chip rise.

text.p: Led by a rise in blue chips, Israeli shares recovered from early losses to close higher on Thursday, traders said.
The benchmark Mishtanim index of the top 100 shares gained 0.76 percent, or 1.80 points, to 239.13 on all-share turnover of 150 million shekels against 200 million shekels on Wednesday.
The Maof 25 blue chip index closed 1.27 percent higher at 248.14.

"The session opened with mild losses, but during the day the market recovered closing slightly higher. The main gainers were the blue chips traded on the Maof, while small capitalization stocks closed lower," said Doron Tsur, head of research at Sahar Securities.

"The market recovered from early losses when investors saw that blue chip stocks were rising. Activity was slightly down today but the market looks very good," said Ari Eidelheit at Zeler Eblagon Securities.

"The market has risen very fast and is expected to continue its positive momentum but at a much slower pace," Tsur said. "During the last few days the market has been mixed and selective. This is a positive sign, showing that the market is stabilizing."

Clal Electronic Industries, the most active share, rose 3.75 percent to 40,311 agorot on volume of 11 million shekels. Traders said the share rose on rumours that Eastman Kodak would acquire the stake of International Paper in Clal's Nasdaq-traded affiliate Scitex Corp.
International Paper on Wednesday said it was taking a $165 million pre-tax charge to write down its investment in Scitex.
A spokesman for Kodak said company policy was not to comment on rumours. "If we had anything to say we would have said it by now," he told Reuters on Thursday.

Other active shares include Koor Industries, which rose 2.25 percent to 33,224 agorot on turnover of 9.5 million shekels, and IDB Holdings, which gained 2.0 percent to 6,542 agorot on volume of 6.8 million shekels.
Osem Investments surged 5.25 percent to 1,837 agorot. Traders said they knew of no reason for the rise.
